Q121: Each class contributes the squared difference between its 0/1 indicator and its predicted probability: 0.25, 0.49 and 0.04. The mean over the three classes is 0.78/3 = 0.26.
Q122: The information score credits the log of the posterior minus the log of the prior of the correct class. Raising 0.3 to 0.9 gains about 1.6 bits; raising 0.8 to 0.9 gains about 0.2 bits.
Q123: In the F-beta score recall is weighted beta times as important as precision. Missing a sick patient is a false negative, so recall must dominate, which needs beta above 1; beta = 0 reduces the score to precision.
Q124: Predicting a class only when very confident minimizes false positives, which raises precision, while more true positives fall below the threshold and become false negatives, which lowers recall.
Q125: A lower threshold classifies more items as positive, so both the true positive rate on the vertical axis and the false positive rate on the horizontal axis increase.
Q126: Precision is true positives over all predicted positives, 80/150 = 0.53. Recall is true positives over all actual positives, 80/100 = 0.80. The 0.91 figure is the accuracy.
Q127: Precision is 40/50 = 0.80 and recall is 40/100 = 0.40. F1 is 2 x 0.80 x 0.40 / 1.20 = 0.53; the arithmetic mean 0.60 overstates it and 0.93 is the accuracy.
Q128: With one class far more frequent, a classifier can reach high accuracy by favoring it while rarely detecting the minority class, so equal class sizes keep the learned boundary from being dominated.
Q129: Drawing n times with replacement picks a given instance at least once with probability about 1 minus 1/e, which is 0.632, so the remaining 36.8% of instances are never drawn and form the test set.
Q130: Random splits from the same data overlap heavily, so the repeated estimates are correlated and give a false sense of diversity. k-fold tests each instance exactly once across the folds.
Q131: Instances from the same person are correlated, so folds that mix a subject's sessions into both training and testing inflate the estimate. Holding out whole subjects removes that inner-subject correlation.
Q132: Feature selection, hyperparameter tuning and testing each need their own data set. Using one set for several purposes lets the test data shape the model, so the reported performance is biased.
Q133: The learned labels are predictions, not ground truth, and there is no guaranteed success. Weighting the samples reduces the dependency of the retrained classifier on those possibly wrong labels.
Q134: Co-training splits the features into independent perspectives, trains one classifier per subset, and iteratively adds the highest-confidence labelled samples of each to the labelled pool until convergence.
Q135: Test outcomes form a Bernoulli process whose estimate tightens with n. The lectures' example gives roughly 0.73 to 0.77 for 1000 samples but 0.69 to 0.80 for 100 samples.
Q136: Normalization fitted on the training input must be applied identically to the test input. Recomputing on the test data would change the scale the model was trained with.
Q137: Outliers should only be discarded with evidence that they are errors. The large claims are real events that dominate what the insurer must predict, so a model built without them is invalid.
Q138: A feature is more relevant the more it separates a sample from samples of other classes and the less it separates it from samples of its own class.
Q139: The volume scales with radius to the power D, so the inner sphere holds (1 - ε)^D of the volume and the shell holds the rest, which approaches all of it in high dimensions.
Q140: This is the peaking phenomenon: the volume of the space grows exponentially with dimension, so a fixed sample becomes too sparse to describe the distribution and predictive power falls.
Q141: With linear activations the error has a global minimum at which the network projects the inputs onto the subspace of the first principal components; nonlinear reduction needs more layers and nonlinear activations.
Q142: The ratio d of projection error to total variation is the lost share, so 100 (1 - d) percent of the variance is retained. Typical choices keep d between 0.01 and 0.05.
Q143: Raising the inner product plus c to a high power sends values below 1 toward 0 and values above 1 toward infinity, which is why degree 2 is usually used.
Q144: The polynomial kernel builds on the inner product, so it captures direction and feature combinations; this suits bag-of-words vectors where co-occurring words matter more than Euclidean distance.
Q145: A one-class SVM takes data from a single class and separates legitimate points maximally from anomalies; the RBF kernel lets it circle the region of feature space where normal samples are expected.
Q146: The Gaussian kernel is near 1 only when the point is close to a landmark and tends to 0 otherwise, so the hypothesis reduces to w0 = -0.5, which is below the threshold of 0.
Q147: Term-document matrices are large and sparse, and mapping documents with the first k singular vectors gives the k-dimensional space with the smallest distance to the original.
Q148: The normalized density is the bin count over N times the bin width: 30 / (200 x 0.5) = 0.30. Dividing only by N gives a probability mass, not a density.
Q149: A histogram only needs the counts per bin, so the raw data items can be thrown away after the histogram is created, unlike instance-based methods that must keep every sample.
Q150: A fixed width is wide relative to the spacing in dense regions, smoothing away structure, and narrow relative to the spacing in sparse regions, where few points fall in the kernel and the estimate is noisy.
Q151: The Parzen window has a fixed size, so K varies with the data. The nearest-neighbour method fixes K and expands the sphere until it contains exactly K points, making the width adapt to local density.
Q152: With a hard window the estimate jumps whenever a sample crosses the window boundary. A smooth kernel such as the Gaussian removes these artificial discontinuities.
Q153: Bayes' theorem with class density K_A / (N_A V), prior N_A / N and evidence K / (N V) gives K_A / K; the class frequencies cancel, so no balancing is needed.
Q154: Splitting perpendicular to the direction of greatest spread at the median leaves half the points on each side; balanced, roughly square regions keep the backtracking cost during search low.
Q155: The leaf region only bounds the query, not its nearest neighbour. A point in an adjacent region can be closer than any point in the leaf, so siblings and, recursively, parents are checked.
Q156: Corners of hyperrectangles may hold points farther from the centre than other regions, forcing many branches to be examined. Ball trees enclose sub-trees in the smallest hypersphere, which has no corners.
Q157: Information gain is the parent entropy minus the weighted entropy of the children, so the split with the lowest child entropy wins: 0.997 - 0.756 = 0.241 for the accelerometer.
Q158: Entropy is minus the sum of p log2 p: 0.8 x 0.32 + 0.2 x 2.32 = 0.72 bits. Only an even split of two classes would reach 1 bit.
Q159: The absence of a value may itself carry information, so a binary feature can record it; alternatively the instance is propagated to all leaves with weights from the training frequencies and the results combined.
Q160: Fully grown trees contain unnecessary structure. When the pessimistic error of the subtree exceeds that of a majority-vote leaf at the parent, the subtree is replaced by that leaf.
Q161: A leaf with 1 error in 2 samples has an upper limit of 0.72 while 2 errors in 6 gives 0.47, so the confidence limit distrusts leaves with little evidence and favors pruning them.
Q162: Bagging reduces variance only when the trees differ. A few strong features would dominate every tree's splits, making the trees correlated and impairing the benefit of bagging.
Q163: The hidden error is the transposed weight matrix times the next layer's error, multiplied element-wise (Hadamard product) by the derivative of the activation at that unit's input.
Q164: If all weights are zero or equal, every unit in a layer receives the same delta during backpropagation and the same update, so the units never learn different features.
Q165: At the output layer the error is activation minus target: 0.9 - 1 = -0.1 and 0.2 - 0 = 0.2. The values 0.09 and 0.16 would be the products a(1 - a), which are not the errors.
Q166: The transposed weights give the direction of the error and the activation derivative its speed; where the activation is flat, the derivative is near zero and little error reaches earlier layers.
Q167: A fully connected layer has a weight per input-output pair, 1000 x 1000. A convolutional layer reuses the same filter at every position, so only its three weights are learned.
Q168: The filter computes the difference of adjacent pixels: similar neighbours give a result near 0, differing neighbours give a large absolute value, so the output marks edges.
Q169: A vanilla network takes an input of fixed size through a fixed number of layers. Recurrent networks apply the same function repeatedly, so they can operate over sequences of vectors.
Q170: A recurrent network combines the state vector with a fixed but learned function in every round. Because the function is reused, the network is not tied to a particular sequence length.
Q171: Plain recurrent networks handle direct temporal dependencies but, with an increasing gap between clue and prediction, become unable to learn the connection; this is what LSTMs were designed to fix.
Q172: A plain recurrent cell repeats a single tanh module. An LSTM is still a recurrent network, but its four layers interact in a specific way designed to remember information for long periods.
Q173: A 2D convolution slides over an image grid; a 3D convolution slides over three axes, which fits videos or 3D medical scans. The lectures note it is seldom used.
Q174: The output units apply a sigmoid to a linear combination of the hidden activations, exactly as logistic regression does on features, except that the features are learned by the earlier layers.
Q175: A large λ makes the squared-weight penalty dominate the loss, so minimizing it shrinks the weights toward zero and the decision function flattens, which reduces variance but raises bias.
Q176: Minus log h tends to infinity as h tends to 0, so assigning near-zero probability to the true class costs far more than a hesitant prediction near 0.5.
Q177: C weights the misclassification costs against the squared-weight term that keeps the margin wide. A very large C punishes every margin violation, so the boundary bends to the training points.
Q178: Both fit a linear function of the inputs, and the lectures note the linear SVM is similar to logistic regression. They differ in the cost: margin-based cost terms versus the logistic (cross-entropy) loss.
Q179: The loss sums y log h plus (1 - y) log (1 - h) over all C outputs, so there is one cost term per output and wrong classes are pushed toward 0 while the true class is pushed toward 1.
Q180: Hyperparameter tuning needs its own data set. Choosing λ on the test set would let the test data shape the model and bias the reported performance.
